title: Ὁ σῦς καὶ ἡ οὐλή
titleEn: The Boar and the Scar — Odyssey 19.403–502
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus's nurse Eurycleia has just set the baby Odysseus on the knees of his grandfather Autolycus, and she asks him to choose a name. Autolycus names the boy Odysseus, from his own anger at many people, and promises gifts when he is grown. The poet tells how Odysseus came to Parnassus for the gifts as a young man, was welcomed by his mother's family, went hunting with Autolycus's sons, and was wounded above the knee by a boar that he killed; they healed him, sent him home with gifts, and he told his parents how he got the scar. Back in the hall, Eurycleia takes his foot, knows the scar, and lets the leg fall into the basin so that the water spills. She tells him she knows him and looks to Penelope, but Athena has turned Penelope's mind aside. Odysseus seizes the nurse by the throat and warns her that he will kill even her with the disloyal maids if she gives him away; she answers that she will keep silent like stone and will tell him which women have wronged him, and he replies that he will find out for himself and bids her trust the gods.

sentences.t:
Αὐτόλυκ’, αὐτὸς νῦν ὄνομ’ εὕρεο ὅττι κε θῆαι
παιδὸς παιδὶ φίλῳ·
sentences.tr:
Autolyk’, autos nyn onom’ heureo hotti ke thēai
paidos paidi philōi·
sentences.l:
“Autolycus, yourself now find a name, whatever you may set
for your child’s child, dear;
sentences.i: “Autolycus, find a name yourself now, whatever name you are to give your dear grandchild;
sentences.n: Eurycleia is speaking: the last part left her setting the baby Odysseus on Autolycus's knees, and these are her words to him. Αὐτόλυκ’ is the vocative with its final ε elided. εὕρεο is the aorist imperative middle of εὑρίσκω 'find' (for yourself), and αὐτός stresses 'you yourself'. ὅττι (= ὅ τι, 'whatever') with κε and the subjunctive θῆαι is an indefinite relative, 'whatever you may set'; θῆαι is a subjunctive of τίθημι, second person singular and middle in form (Attic θῇ), and ὄνομα τίθεσθαι is the idiom 'give a name'. παιδὸς παιδί is 'to a child's child', the grandchild, and 'your' is understood; φίλῳ 'dear' agrees with παιδί.

sentences.t: πολυάρητος δέ τοί ἐστιν.
sentences.tr: polyarētos de toi estin.
sentences.l: and much-prayed-for to you he is.”
sentences.i: for he is much prayed for by you.”
sentences.n: She gives her reason, and her speech ends. τοί is the enclitic dative 'to you' (= σοι), or possibly the particle 'indeed'; read as the dative, with a verbal adjective it names the one who prays, 'much prayed for by you'. πολυάρητος is built from πολύ- 'much' and ἀρή 'prayer' (ἀράομαι 'pray for'), and its sense is passive: a child for whom prayers have been made, not one prayed to. δέ is explanatory, 'for'. Autolycus answers in the next unit.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτ’ Αὐτόλυκος ἀπαμείβετο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ aut’ Autolykos apameibeto phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: Her then in turn answered Autolycus, and spoke:
sentences.i: Then Autolycus answered her in turn, and spoke:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ αὖτ’ … ἀπαμείβετο φώνησέν τε is a reply-formula with the speaker's name filled in. τήν is the pronoun 'her' (Eurycleia; in Homer the 'article' is a pronoun), αὖτε 'in turn' (elided αὖτ’), ἀπαμείβετο the imperfect middle of ἀπαμείβομαι 'answer', and φώνησεν the aorist of φωνέω 'speak'; the second verb adds 'and spoke', and the speech follows.

sentences.t: γαμβρὸς ἐμὸς θυγάτηρ τε, τίθεσθ’ ὄνομ’ ὅττι κεν εἴπω·
sentences.tr: gambros emos thygatēr te, tithesth’ onom’ hotti ken eipō·
sentences.l: “Son-in-law mine and daughter, set a name, whatever I shall say;
sentences.i: “My son-in-law and my daughter, give him whatever name I tell you;
sentences.n: Autolycus speaks, and he addresses the child's parents together: γαμβρός 'son-in-law' (the husband of his daughter; the word covers any man related by marriage) and θυγάτηρ 'daughter' are both vocatives in function but nominatives in form (the true vocative of θυγάτηρ would be θύγατερ), as Homer often has it. τίθεσθε is the present imperative middle of τίθημι, and ὄνομα τίθεσθαι 'give a name' takes the middle because parents name their own child. ὅττι κεν εἴπω is an indefinite relative again (as in 403), with the aorist subjunctive εἴπω 'I shall say'; 'whatever name I tell you'.

sentences.t:
πολλοῖσιν γὰρ ἐγώ γε ὀδυσσάμενος τόδ’ ἱκάνω,
ἀνδράσιν ἠδὲ γυναιξὶν ἀνὰ χθόνα πουλυβότειραν·
sentences.tr:
polloisin gar egō ge odyssamenos tod’ hikanō,
andrasin ēde gynaixin ana chthona poulyboteiran·
sentences.l:
for with many, I, for my part, having been angry, to this have come,
with men and women over the much-nourishing earth;
sentences.i: for I have come to this, angry as I have been with many, men and women, over the earth that feeds so many;
sentences.n: He explains the name he will give: it comes from his anger. ὀδυσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ὀδύσσομαι 'be angry with, hate'; πολλοῖσιν is the dative of those it was felt against, filled out by ἀνδράσιν ἠδὲ γυναιξίν 'men and women'. The participle may be active ('angry with') or passive ('hated by'), which is disputed; its root is that of Ὀδυσεύς in the next unit. τόδ’ ἱκάνω is hard: ἱκάνω is 'I come, I have come' and τόδε is 'to this', and whether this means this place, moment or condition is not clear, so the English stays as vague as the Greek. ἐγώ γε is 'I for my part'. ἀνὰ χθόνα is 'over the earth'; πουλυβότειραν 'much-nourishing' (πολύς + βόσκω 'feed') is a stock epithet of it.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς ὄνομ’ ἔστω ἐπώνυμον·
sentences.tr: tōi d’ Odyseus onom’ estō epōnymon·
sentences.l: therefore let Odysseus be the name, name-bearing;
sentences.i: so let his name be Odysseus, named for this;
sentences.n: The name is given. τῷ is 'therefore, for that reason' (a dative used as an adverb), and the δέ after it is a loose 'and'. ἔστω is the third-person imperative of εἰμί, 'let it be'. Ὀδυσεύς has a single σ here, as Ὀδυσῆϊ did in 416; Homer writes Ὀδυσ- and Ὀδυσσ- as the metre needs. ἐπώνυμον 'name-bearing' is an adjective for a name taken from something (ἐπί 'upon' + ὄνομα): here the name is drawn from ὀδυσσάμενος 'having been angry', which it resembles in sound. The poet states no more than that link.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγώ γε,
ὁππότ’ ἂν ἡβήσας μητρώϊον ἐς μέγα δῶμα
ἔλθῃ Παρνησόνδ’, ὅθι πού μοι κτήματ’ ἔασι,
τῶν οἱ ἐγὼ δώσω καί μιν χαίροντ’ ἀποπέμψω.
sentences.tr:
autar egō ge,
hoppot’ an hēbēsas mētrōïon es mega dōma
elthēi Parnēsond’, hothi pou moi ktēmat’ easi,
tōn hoi egō dōsō kai min chairont’ apopempsō.
sentences.l:
but I, for my part,
whenever, having come of age, to his mother’s great house
he comes, to Parnassus, where possessions of mine are, I suppose,
of these to him I will give, and him rejoicing I will send away.”
sentences.i: but when he has grown to manhood and comes to his mother’s great house on Parnassus, where my possessions are, I suppose, I will give him some of them and send him off rejoicing.”
sentences.n: Autolycus promises gifts for the day the boy is grown, and his speech ends. ὁππότ’ ἄν with the aorist subjunctive ἔλθῃ is 'whenever he comes' (ἄν = κε); ἡβήσας is the aorist participle of ἡβάω 'come to youth, reach manhood'. μητρώϊον is 'of his mother': the house is that of his mother's family, Autolycus's own, named from the boy's side. Παρνησόνδ’ has the suffix -δε 'towards' and is an accusative of goal, 'to Parnassus'. ὅθι πού is 'where, I suppose', a modest way of speaking of his own wealth; ἔασι is the epic form of εἰσί 'are', and κτήματα is 'possessions'. τῶν is partitive, 'some of these'; οἱ is 'to him' and μιν 'him', and χαίροντα is predicative, 'send him away rejoicing'. δώσω and ἀποπέμψω are futures.

sentences.t: τῶν ἕνεκ’ ἦλθ’ Ὀδυσεύς, ἵνα οἱ πόροι ἀγλαὰ δῶρα.
sentences.tr: tōn henek’ ēlth’ Odyseus, hina hoi poroi aglaa dōra.
sentences.l: For the sake of these came Odysseus, that to him he might give splendid gifts.
sentences.i: It was for these that Odysseus came, so that Autolycus might give him splendid gifts.
sentences.n: The narrator's voice returns, in the account of how Odysseus came by his scar that began before this part. τῶν ἕνεκα 'for the sake of these' looks back to the κτήματα of the speech: the gifts promised were the reason for the visit. ἦλθ’ is ἦλθε. πόροι is the aorist optative of πόρον, the old aorist 'gave', and the optative gives purpose after a past tense, 'so that he might give'. Its subject is not stated; it is Autolycus, and οἱ is 'to him', Odysseus. ἀγλαά 'splendid' is the house rendering of ἀγλαός.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἄρ’ Αὐτόλυκός τε καὶ υἱέες Αὐτολύκοιο
χερσίν τ’ ἠσπάζοντο ἔπεσσί τε μειλιχίοισι·
sentences.tr:
ton men ar’ Autolykos te kai huiees Autolykoio
chersin t’ ēspazonto epessi te meilichioisi·
sentences.l:
Him then Autolycus and the sons of Autolycus
with hands were greeting, and with words gentle;
sentences.i: Autolycus and the sons of Autolycus greeted him with their hands and with gentle words;
sentences.n: Odysseus's welcome on Parnassus has two halves: the men greet him here, and his grandmother in the next unit. τὸν μὲν ἄρα: τόν is the pronoun 'him', and μέν looks forward to the δέ of the next line. ἠσπάζοντο is the imperfect middle of ἀσπάζομαι 'greet, welcome', with the augment lengthened to ἠ-; 'with their hands' means by clasping and embracing. ἔπεσσι μειλιχίοισι is a dative plural in -εσσι and -οισι (Attic -εσι, -οις), and μειλίχιος is 'gentle'. Αὐτολύκοιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου).

sentences.t:
μήτηρ δ’ Ἀμφιθέη μητρὸς περιφῦσ’ Ὀδυσῆϊ
κύσσ’ ἄρα μιν κεφαλήν τε καὶ ἄμφω φάεα καλά.
sentences.tr:
mētēr d’ Amphitheē mētros periphys’ Odysēï
kyss’ ara min kephalēn te kai amphō phaea kala.
sentences.l:
and the mother, Amphithea, of his mother, having clung round Odysseus,
kissed him then, on the head and on both his fine eyes.
sentences.i: and his mother’s mother, Amphithea, threw her arms about Odysseus and kissed him on the head and on both his beautiful eyes.
sentences.n: μήτηρ … μητρός is 'the mother of his mother', his grandmother, with her name Ἀμφιθέη set between the two words. περιφῦσ’ is the aorist participle περιφῦσα, literally 'having grown round', that is clinging to, and takes the dative Ὀδυσῆϊ. κύσσ’ is κύσσε, the aorist of κυνέω 'kiss', without augment, and ἄρα 'then'. κεφαλήν and φάεα are accusatives of the parts kissed, beside μιν 'him': 'him, on the head and both eyes'. φάεα, literally 'lights', is the epic word for 'eyes'. καλά is 'fine' by the house rendering ('beautiful' in the i layer).

sentences.t:
Αὐτόλυκος δ’ υἱοῖσιν ἐκέκλετο κυδαλίμοισι
δεῖπνον ἐφοπλίσσαι·
sentences.tr:
Autolykos d’ huioisin ekekleto kydalimoisi
deipnon ephoplissai·
sentences.l:
And Autolycus to his sons, glorious ones, called out
a meal to make ready;
sentences.i: Autolycus gave orders to his glorious sons to make ready a meal;
sentences.n: The feast begins with an order. ἐκέκλετο is the reduplicated aorist middle of κέλομαι 'call to, urge', 'called out' or 'gave orders'; the dative υἱοῖσιν 'to his sons' names those ordered, and the infinitive ἐφοπλίσσαι (ἐφοπλίζω 'make ready'; the doubled σ is for the metre) says what they are to do. κυδαλίμοισι 'glorious' is a stock epithet, built on κῦδος 'glory'. δεῖπνον is 'meal', with no time of day attached.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ὀτρύνοντος ἄκουσαν,
αὐτίκα δ’ εἰσάγαγον βοῦν ἄρσενα πενταέτηρον·
sentences.tr:
toi d’ otrynontos akousan,
autika d’ eisagagon boun arsena pentaetēron·
sentences.l:
and they heeded him urging,
and at once led in an ox, a male, five-year-old;
sentences.i: and they obeyed his urging, and at once led in a five-year-old male ox;
sentences.n: τοί is the pronoun 'they', the sons. ἄκουσαν is ἤκουσαν without its augment, the aorist of ἀκούω, and ἀκούω takes the genitive of the person heard, here the participle ὀτρύνοντος 'urging': 'they heard him urging' is 'they heeded him'. εἰσάγαγον is the aorist of εἰσάγω 'lead in' (no augment), and the animal is brought in alive to be killed. βοῦν ἄρσενα is 'a male ox' and πενταέτηρον 'five-year-old' (πέντε + ἔτος).

sentences.t:
τὸν δέρον ἀμφί θ’ ἕπον, καί μιν διέχευαν ἅπαντα,
μίστυλλόν τ’ ἄρ’ ἐπισταμένως πεῖράν τ’ ὀβελοῖσιν,
ὤπτησάν τε περιφραδέως, δάσσαντό τε μοίρας.
sentences.tr:
ton deron amphi th’ hepon, kai min diecheuan hapanta,
mistyllon t’ ar’ epistamenōs peiran t’ obeloisin,
ōptēsan te periphradeōs, dassanto te moiras.
sentences.l:
him they flayed and dressed, and cut him up, all of him,
and cut into pieces skilfully and pierced on spits,
and roasted very carefully, and divided the portions.
sentences.i: they flayed it and dressed the carcass, and cut up the whole of it, and cut the meat skilfully into small pieces and pierced them on spits, and roasted them with great care, and divided out the portions.
sentences.n: The butchery is told in the order it is done, one verb after another: flaying, dressing, cutting up, slicing, spitting, roasting, sharing out. τὸν is the pronoun 'it', the ox; δέρον is the unaugmented imperfect of δέρω 'flay'; ἀμφί … ἕπον is a tmesis of ἀμφέπω 'attend to, work at', which with δέρω is 'dress' the carcass; διέχευαν is the aorist of διαχέω, literally 'pour apart', here 'cut up', and ἅπαντα 'all (of it)'. μίστυλλον is the imperfect of μιστύλλω 'cut into small pieces', ἐπισταμένως 'skilfully' (from ἐπίσταμαι 'know how'), and πεῖραν is ἔπειραν without augment, from πείρω 'pierce', here 'on spits' (ὀβελοῖσιν). ὤπτησαν is from ὀπτάω 'roast', περιφραδέως 'with careful thought' (περί + φράζομαι), and δάσσαντο the aorist middle of δατέομαι 'divide among themselves'. μοῖρα is 'portion'.

sentences.t:
ὣς τότε μὲν πρόπαν ἦμαρ ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα
δαίνυντ’, οὐδέ τι θυμὸς ἐδεύετο δαιτὸς ἐΐσης·
sentences.tr:
hōs tote men propan ēmar es ēelion katadynta
dainynt’, oude ti thymos edeueto daitos eïsēs·
sentences.l:
So then for the whole day, until the sun going down,
feasted, and not at all did the heart lack the equal feast;
sentences.i: So for that whole day, until the sun went down, they feasted, and their hearts went short of nothing in the equally shared feast;
sentences.n: The feast runs from the butchery to sunset, and 'the equal feast' is one in which every guest has an equal share. πρόπαν ἦμαρ is 'the whole day'; ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα is 'until the sun going down' (the participle is the aorist καταδύντα, 'having set'); δαίνυντ’ is the unaugmented δαίνυντο, 'they feasted'. θυμός is the heart as the seat of appetite, and ἐδεύετο, the imperfect of δεύομαι 'lack, be in want of', takes the genitive δαιτός. ἐΐσης 'equal' is the genitive singular feminine of ἐΐσος (the same word as ἴσος), agreeing with δαιτός.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠέλιος κατέδυ καὶ ἐπὶ κνέφας ἦλθεν,
δὴ τότε κοιμήσαντο καὶ ὕπνου δῶρον ἕλοντο.
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ēelios katedy kai epi knephas ēlthen,
dē tote koimēsanto kai hypnou dōron helonto.
sentences.l:
and when the sun set and darkness came on,
then indeed they lay down to sleep and took the gift of sleep.
sentences.i: and when the sun set and darkness came on, then they lay down to sleep and took the gift of sleep.
sentences.n: Evening follows the feast, in two lines. ἦμος is 'when', and the subject of ἦλθεν 'came' is κνέφας 'darkness'; κατέδυ is the aorist of καταδύω 'go down, set'. δὴ τότε 'then indeed' answers ἦμος. κοιμήσαντο is the aorist middle of κοιμάω 'put to sleep', so 'put themselves to sleep, lay down', and ὕπνου δῶρον ἕλοντο 'took the gift of sleep' presents sleep as something given (ἕλοντο is the aorist middle of αἱρέω, 'took for themselves').

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
βάν ῥ’ ἴμεν ἐς θήρην, ἠμὲν κύνες ἠδὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ
υἱέες Αὐτολύκου·
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ērigeneia phanē rhododaktylos Ēōs,
ban rh’ imen es thērēn, ēmen kynes ēde kai autoi
huiees Autolykou·
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, the dogs and the sons of Autolycus themselves set out for the hunt;
sentences.n: A new day and a new scene: the hunting party leaves. The dawn line is a formula whose epithets are translated each time: ἠριγένεια 'early-born' (ἠρι- 'early' + the root of γίγνομαι) and ῥοδοδάκτυλος 'rose-fingered'. βάν is ἔβαν without augment, the aorist of βαίνω, and ῥ’ is ἄρα; ἴμεν is the infinitive of εἶμι 'go', so βάν ῥ’ ἴμεν is 'set out to go', and ἐς θήρην 'for the hunt'. ἠμὲν … ἠδὲ καί … is 'both … and also': the dogs go as well as the men, and αὐτοί 'themselves' marks the men in person, as against the dogs. υἱέες Αὐτολύκου is the nominative plural in -εες (Attic υἱοί).

sentences.t:
μετὰ τοῖσι δὲ δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἤϊεν·
sentences.tr:
meta toisi de dios Odysseus
ēïen·
sentences.l:
and among them heavenly Odysseus
went;
sentences.i: and heavenly Odysseus went among them;
sentences.n: μετά with the dative τοῖσι is 'among them': Odysseus goes with the sons of Autolycus. δῖος is 'heavenly' by the house rendering, a stock epithet of Odysseus. ἤϊεν is the imperfect of εἶμι 'go'. The same half-line comes again at 437–438, when the party has reached the glen.

sentences.t:
αἰπὺ δ’ ὄρος προσέβαν καταειμένον ὕλῃ
Παρνησοῦ, τάχα δ’ ἵκανον πτύχας ἠνεμοέσσας.
sentences.tr:
aipy d’ oros proseban kataeimenon hylēi
Parnēsou, tacha d’ hikanon ptychas ēnemoessas.
sentences.l:
and the steep mountain they climbed, clothed in forest,
of Parnassus, and soon they came to the windy folds.
sentences.i: and they climbed the steep mountain of Parnassus, clothed in forest, and soon reached its windy folds.
sentences.n: The party climbs Parnassus, and the poet names the mountain only after describing it. προσέβαν is the aorist of προσβαίνω 'go up to, climb', without augment (ἔβαν is the Homeric form beside ἔβησαν). αἰπύ 'steep' and ὄρος 'mountain' belong together, and the genitive Παρνησοῦ 'of Parnassus' (Attic Παρνασσός) names it; καταειμένον, the perfect passive participle of καταέννυμι 'clothe', is 'clothed', and ὕλῃ is 'forest, woodland'. πτύχες, literally 'folds', are the valleys and recesses in the mountain's flank, and ἠνεμόεις 'windy' is built on ἄνεμος 'wind'. ἵκανον is from ἱκάνω 'come to, reach'.

sentences.t:
Ἠέλιος μὲν ἔπειτα νέον προσέβαλλεν ἀρούρας
ἐξ ἀκαλαρρείταο βαθυρρόου Ὠκεανοῖο,
οἱ δ’ ἐς βῆσσαν ἵκανον ἐπακτῆρες·
sentences.tr:
Ēelios men epeita neon proseballen arouras
ex akalarreitao bathyrroou Ōkeanoio,
hoi d’ es bēssan hikanon epaktēres·
sentences.i: The Sun was just then striking the fields, out of gently flowing, deep-flowing Oceanus, and the hunters came into a glen;
sentences.n: The time of day is early morning: the Sun has just risen out of Oceanus, the great stream at the edge of the world, and its light is falling on the fields. νέον is 'newly, just now'; προσέβαλλεν is the imperfect of προσβάλλω 'strike against'; ἀρούρας is 'ploughed fields'. ἐξ ἀκαλαρρείταο βαθυρρόου Ὠκεανοῖο has genitives in -αο and -οιο (Attic -ου), and the two epithets are 'gently flowing' (ἀκαλός 'quiet, gentle' + ῥέω 'flow') and 'deep-flowing' (βαθύς 'deep' + ῥόος 'stream'). οἱ δέ 'they' are the hunters, ἐπακτῆρες, a word built on ἐπάγω 'bring on', the verb that appears as ἐπάγοντες at 445: they are those who set the dogs on. ἐς βῆσσαν is 'into a glen', a wooded valley.

sentences.t:
πρὸ δ’ ἄρ’ αὐτῶν
ἴχνι’ ἐρευνῶντες κύνες ἤϊσαν, αὐτὰρ ὄπισθεν
υἱέες Αὐτολύκου·
sentences.tr:
pro d’ ar’ autōn
ichni’ ereunōntes kynes ēïsan, autar opisthen
huiees Autolykou·
sentences.i: and in front of them the dogs went, searching out the tracks, and behind them came the sons of Autolycus;
sentences.n: The order of the hunt: dogs in front, tracking, then the sons of Autolycus, and in the next unit Odysseus close by the dogs. πρὸ δέ 'and in front' takes αὐτῶν 'of them' (genitive after πρό); ἴχνι’ is ἴχνια 'tracks, footprints', elided; ἐρευνῶντες 'searching out' is the participle of ἐρευνάω; ἤϊσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι 'go' in its -σαν form. αὐτὰρ ὄπισθεν 'but behind' has no verb of its own, and 'went' is carried over from the clause before. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
μετὰ τοῖσι δὲ δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἤϊεν ἄγχι κυνῶν, κραδάων δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος.
sentences.tr:
meta toisi de dios Odysseus
ēïen anchi kynōn, kradaōn dolichoskion enchos.
sentences.l:
and among them heavenly Odysseus
went close by the dogs, brandishing a long-shadowed spear.
sentences.i: and heavenly Odysseus went among them, close by the dogs, brandishing his long-shadowed spear.
sentences.n: The first half-line repeats 430–431 word for word, and the English does the same. ἄγχι κυνῶν is 'close by the dogs' (ἄγχι takes the genitive), and κραδάων 'brandishing' is the participle of κραδάω, a by-form of κραδαίνω 'shake, swing'. δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος is 'a long-shadowed spear': δολιχός 'long' + σκιά 'shadow', and the likely sense is a spear that throws a long shadow, that is a long spear. ἔγχος and δόρυ both mean 'spear'.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δ’ ἄρ’ ἐν λόχμῃ πυκινῇ κατέκειτο μέγας σῦς·
sentences.tr: entha d’ ar’ en lochmēi pykinēi katekeito megas sys·
sentences.l: There then in a thick covert lay a great boar:
sentences.i: There in a thick covert lay a great boar:
sentences.n: The hunters come on their quarry. ἔνθα is local, 'there'. λόχμη is a 'covert', the thicket or hollow in which an animal lies hidden; the word is built on the root of λόχος 'ambush'. κατέκειτο is the imperfect of κατάκειμαι 'lie', and πυκινῇ is 'thick'. μέγας σῦς 'a great boar' is the boar that left the scar, named at 393 in the last part and now seen for the first time in the story of the hunt. The three lines that follow say how thick the covert is.

sentences.t:
τὴν μὲν ἄρ’ οὔτ’ ἀνέμων διάει μένος ὑγρὸν ἀέντων,
οὔτε μιν Ἠέλιος φαέθων ἀκτῖσιν ἔβαλλεν,
οὔτ’ ὄμβρος περάασκε διαμπερές·
sentences.tr:
tēn men ar’ out’ anemōn diaei menos hygron aentōn,
oute min Ēelios phaethōn aktisin eballen,
out’ ombros peraaske diamperes·
sentences.i: Neither did the moist force of blowing winds blow through it, nor did the shining Sun strike it with his rays, nor did rain pass right through;
sentences.n: Three negatives (οὔτε … οὔτε … οὔτ’) show that the covert let in neither wind, sun nor rain. τήν is 'it', the covert (λόχμη is feminine), and μιν in the next line is the same 'it'. διάει is from διάημι 'blow through', and ἀέντων is the genitive plural participle of ἄημι 'blow', agreeing with ἀνέμων 'of winds'; the repeated idea of wind is for emphasis, and μένος ὑγρόν is 'the wet (moist) force'. φαέθων 'shining' is a stock epithet of the Sun, and Ἠέλιος the Ionic form of Ἥλιος. περάασκε is an iterative imperfect of περάω 'pass through' ('used to pass'), here the standing property of the covert, and διαμπερές 'right through'.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα πυκνὴ
ἦεν, ἀτὰρ φύλλων ἐνέην χύσις ἤλιθα πολλή.
sentences.tr:
hōs ara pyknē
ēen, atar phyllōn eneēn chysis ēlitha pollē.
sentences.l:
so then thick
it was, and moreover of leaves in it was a heap exceedingly great.
sentences.i: so thick was it, and besides, there was in it a very great heap of leaves.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα πυκνὴ ἦεν 'so thick it was' sums up the three negatives: πυκνή is the feminine of πυκινός 'thick', and ἦεν is ἦν. ἀτάρ is 'and yet, and moreover'. ἐνέην is the epic imperfect of ἔνειμι 'be in' (Attic ἐνῆν); φύλλων is 'of leaves' and χύσις 'a heap' (from χέω 'pour', so literally 'a pouring'), and ἤλιθα 'exceedingly' goes with πολλή 'great'. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἀνδρῶν τε κυνῶν τε περὶ κτύπος ἦλθε ποδοῖϊν,
ὡς ἐπάγοντες ἐπῇσαν·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ andrōn te kynōn te peri ktypos ēlthe podoiïn,
hōs epagontes epēisan·
sentences.l:
And him, of men and of dogs, about came the thud of feet,
as, setting-on, they came on;
sentences.i: Around him came the sound of the feet of men and dogs, as they came on, setting the dogs on;
sentences.n: The boar hears the hunters. τόν is 'him', the boar, and περί … ἦλθε is a tmesis of περιῆλθε, 'came round'. κτύπος is 'thud, din', and ποδοῖϊν is a dual form (Attic ποδοῖν), here simply 'of feet'; ἀνδρῶν τε κυνῶν τε is 'of men and of dogs'. ὡς ἐπάγοντες ἐπῇσαν: ὡς is 'as', ἐπάγοντες 'bringing on' (the verb behind ἐπακτῆρες at 435), and ἐπῇσαν the imperfect of ἔπειμι 'come on, approach'. The object of ἐπάγοντες is not stated; 'setting the dogs on' is the usual hunting sense.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἀντίος ἐκ ξυλόχοιο
φρίξας εὖ λοφιήν, πῦρ δ’ ὀφθαλμοῖσι δεδορκώς,
στῆ ῥ’ αὐτῶν σχεδόθεν·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ antios ek xylochoio
phrixas eu lophiēn, pyr d’ ophthalmoisi dedorkōs,
stē rh’ autōn schedothen·
sentences.i: and he, facing them out of the lair, his crest bristling high and fire in his glaring eyes, stood close before them;
sentences.n: The boar comes out to meet the hunters. ὁ δέ 'and he' marks the change of subject back to the boar; ἀντίος 'facing' agrees with ὁ, and ἐκ ξυλόχοιο is 'out of the lair' (ξύλοχος, from ξύλον 'wood' and λόχος 'ambush', is a thicket where a beast lies). φρίξας is the aorist participle of φρίσσω 'bristle', εὖ 'well, fully', and λοφιήν is the ridge of stiff bristles down a boar's back, here 'crest'. πῦρ ὀφθαλμοῖσι δεδορκώς: δεδορκώς is the perfect participle of δέρκομαι 'look', with the accusative πῦρ, so 'looking fire', that is glaring with fire in his eyes. στῆ ῥ’ is ἔστη ἄρα, 'he stood'; αὐτῶν σχεδόθεν is 'near them' (σχεδόθεν takes the genitive).

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἄρα πρώτιστος Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἔσσυτ’ ἀνασχόμενος δολιχὸν δόρυ χειρὶ παχείῃ,
οὐτάμεναι μεμαώς·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ara prōtistos Odysseus
essyt’ anaschomenos dolichon dory cheiri pacheiēi,
outamenai memaōs·
sentences.i: but Odysseus was the first of all to rush at him, raising his long spear in his stout hand, eager to wound it;
sentences.n: Odysseus is first to charge. ὁ δ’ ἄρα is 'and he', with Ὀδυσσεύς added to name him, and πρώτιστος is the superlative 'first of all'. ἔσσυτο is the aorist middle of σεύω 'rush, hurry', with the doubled σ the verb takes in this form. ἀνασχόμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἀνέχω 'hold up, raise'; δολιχὸν δόρυ is 'a long spear', and χειρὶ παχείῃ 'with his stout hand' (παχύς 'thick, stout'). οὐτάμεναι is the aorist infinitive of οὐτάω 'wound, thrust at', in the older -μεναι form (Attic -ναι), and μεμαώς is the perfect participle of μέμονα 'be eager'.

sentences.t:
ὁ δέ μιν φθάμενος ἔλασεν σῦς
γουνὸς ὕπερ, πολλὸν δὲ διήφυσε σαρκὸς ὀδόντι
λικριφὶς ἀΐξας, οὐδ’ ὀστέον ἵκετο φωτός.
sentences.tr:
ho de min phthamenos elasen sys
gounos hyper, pollon de diēphyse sarkos odonti
likriphis aïxas, oud’ osteon hiketo phōtos.
sentences.l:
but him forestalling struck the boar
above the knee, and much of the flesh he tore through with his tooth,
darting aslant, and he did not reach the bone of the man.
sentences.i: but the boar got in first and struck him above the knee, and darting aslant it tore through much of the flesh with its tusk, though it did not reach the man’s bone.
sentences.n: The boar is quicker than Odysseus and wounds him, and this is the origin of the scar. ὁ δέ 'but he' is the boar, named by σῦς at the end of 449; φθάμενος is the aorist middle participle of φθάνω 'get in first, forestall', with μιν 'him'. ἔλασεν, the aorist of ἐλαύνω, is 'struck' (a blow dealt); γουνός is the genitive of γόνυ 'knee', which ὕπερ 'above' governs. πολλὸν … σαρκός is 'much of the flesh' (a partitive genitive), and διήφυσε, the aorist of διαφύσσω 'draw through, rip open', is the tearing; ὀδόντι is 'with a tooth', the boar's tusk. λικριφίς 'aslant, sideways' is an adverb, and ἀΐξας the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω 'dart'. φωτός is the genitive of φώς 'man'.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς οὔτησε τυχὼν κατὰ δεξιὸν ὦμον,
ἀντικρὺ δὲ διῆλθε φαεινοῦ δουρὸς ἀκωκή·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ Odyseus outēse tychōn kata dexion ōmon,
antikry de diēlthe phaeinou douros akōkē·
sentences.l:
And him Odysseus wounded, having hit him on the right shoulder,
and straight through went the point of the shining spear;
sentences.i: But Odysseus hit him true, wounding him on the right shoulder, and the point of his shining spear went clean through;
sentences.n: Odysseus's own thrust follows. τὸν δ’ Ὀδυσεύς is 'and him Odysseus'; οὔτησε is the aorist of οὐτάω 'wound', the verb of οὐτάμεναι above, and τυχών the aorist participle of τυγχάνω 'hit the mark'. κατὰ δεξιὸν ὦμον is 'on the right shoulder' (literally 'down along'), and ἀντικρύ 'straight through'. The subject of διῆλθε 'went through' is ἀκωκή 'point', and φαεινοῦ δουρός 'of the shining spear' (δουρός is the genitive of δόρυ) says whose point. φαεινός is 'shining' by the house rendering.

sentences.t: κὰδ δ’ ἔπεσ’ ἐν κονίῃσι μακών, ἀπὸ δ’ ἔπτατο θυμός.
sentences.tr: kad d’ epes’ en koniēisi makōn, apo d’ eptato thymos.
sentences.l: and down he fell in the dust, crying out, and away flew his life.
sentences.i: he fell down in the dust with a cry, and his life flew away.
sentences.n: The subject is the boar: it falls, and its life leaves it. κάδ is κατά with its last letter assimilated to the following δ, so κὰδ δ’ ἔπεσ’ is κατὰ δὲ ἔπεσε 'and down it fell'. μακών is the aorist participle of μηκάομαι, a verb for the cry of an animal, so 'crying out'. ἀπὸ δ’ ἔπτατο is a tmesis of ἀπέπτατο, 'flew away'. θυμός, which is usually 'heart', is what leaves the body at death and is rendered 'life' here. The line is one of Homer's stock lines for a death.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἄρ’ Αὐτολύκου παῖδες φίλοι ἀμφεπένοντο,
ὠτειλὴν δ’ Ὀδυσῆος ἀμύμονος ἀντιθέοιο
δῆσαν ἐπισταμένως, ἐπαοιδῇ δ’ αἷμα κελαινὸν
ἔσχεθον, αἶψα δ’ ἵκοντο φίλου πρὸς δώματα πατρός.
sentences.tr:
ton men ar’ Autolykou paides philoi amphepenonto,
ōteilēn d’ Odysēos amymonos antitheoio
dēsan epistamenōs, epaoidēi d’ haima kelainon
eschethon, aipsa d’ hikonto philou pros dōmata patros.
sentences.l:
Him then of Autolycus the dear sons were attending,
and the wound of Odysseus, blameless, godlike,
they bound skilfully, and by incantation the dark blood
they held back, and quickly they came to the house of their dear father.
sentences.i: Autolycus’ dear sons attended to him, and bound the wound of blameless, godlike Odysseus skilfully, and with an incantation checked the dark blood, and quickly they came to the house of their dear father.
sentences.n: The sons of Autolycus treat the wound before they take him home. τὸν is 'him', Odysseus; ἀμφεπένοντο is the imperfect of ἀμφιπένομαι 'busy oneself about, attend to', and φίλοι 'dear' is said of the sons. ὠτειλήν 'wound' is the object of δῆσαν, 'they bound', and ἐπισταμένως 'skilfully'. ἐπαοιδή, from ἐπᾴδω 'sing over', is an incantation spoken over a wound, and the poet gives no words; ἔσχεθον is a form of the aorist of ἔχω with an added θ, 'they held back', and αἷμα κελαινόν is 'dark blood'. ἀμύμων is rendered 'blameless', but its real meaning is not known; ἀντίθεος is 'godlike', literally 'a match for a god'. αἶψα 'quickly'; ἵκοντο is the aorist middle of ἱκνέομαι 'come'; φίλου … πατρός is 'of their dear father'.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἄρ’ Αὐτόλυκός τε καὶ υἱέες Αὐτολύκοιο
εὖ ἰησάμενοι ἠδ’ ἀγλαὰ δῶρα πορόντες
καρπαλίμως χαίροντα φίλην ἐς πατρίδ’ ἔπεμπον
εἰς Ἰθάκην.
sentences.tr:
ton men ar’ Autolykos te kai huiees Autolykoio
eu iēsamenoi ēd’ aglaa dōra porontes
karpalimōs chaironta philēn es patrid’ epempon
eis Ithakēn.
sentences.l:
Him then Autolycus and the sons of Autolycus,
having healed him well and splendid gifts having given,
speedily rejoicing to his dear fatherland were sending,
to Ithaca.
sentences.i: Autolycus and the sons of Autolycus healed him well, gave him splendid gifts, and speedily sent him, rejoicing, to his dear fatherland, to Ithaca.
sentences.n: The visit ends. The opening of the line repeats the opening of the welcome at 414, so that the same men who greeted him now send him home. ἰησάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ἰάομαι 'heal', and πορόντες the aorist participle of the old verb πόρον 'give' (as in πόροι at 413); ἀγλαὰ δῶρα 'splendid gifts' is the fulfilment of Autolycus's promise. καρπαλίμως is 'speedily'; χαίροντα 'rejoicing' is what Autolycus said at 412; ἔπεμπον is the imperfect of πέμπω 'send'. φίλην ἐς πατρίδ’ is 'to his dear fatherland', and εἰς Ἰθάκην 'to Ithaca' is in apposition.

sentences.t:
τῷ μέν ῥα πατὴρ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ
χαῖρον νοστήσαντι καὶ ἐξερέεινον ἕκαστα,
οὐλὴν ὅττι πάθοι·
sentences.tr:
tōi men rha patēr kai potnia mētēr
chairon nostēsanti kai exereeinon hekasta,
oulēn hotti pathoi·
sentences.i: His father and lady mother were glad at his homecoming, and asked him about every detail, how he had come by the scar;
sentences.n: Odysseus's parents receive him. τῷ is 'at him' (the person one rejoices at, after χαῖρον), and νοστήσαντι is the dative aorist participle of νοστέω 'come home': 'rejoiced at him as he came home'. πότνια is 'lady', a title of respect. ἐξερέεινον is the imperfect of ἐξερεείνω 'ask about, inquire into', and ἕκαστα is 'each thing, every detail'. The question is given as οὐλὴν ὅττι πάθοι, 'the scar, what he had suffered': οὐλήν 'scar' is put ahead of the clause, and πάθοι is an optative in an indirect question after a past tense. The sense is 'how he came by the scar', and the next unit gives the answer.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἄρα σφίσιν εὖ κατέλεξεν
ὥς μιν θηρεύοντ’ ἔλασεν σῦς λευκῷ ὀδόντι,
Παρνησόνδ’ ἐλθόντα σὺν υἱάσιν Αὐτολύκοιο.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ara sphisin eu katelexen
hōs min thēreuont’ elasen sys leukōi odonti,
Parnēsond’ elthonta syn huiasin Autolykoio.
sentences.l:
and he then to them well recounted
how him hunting struck a boar with a white tooth,
having gone to Parnassus with the sons of Autolycus.
sentences.i: and he told them the whole story: how a boar had struck him with its white tusk while he was hunting, when he had gone to Parnassus with the sons of Autolycus.
sentences.n: He answers their question, and the story of the scar ends. ὁ is 'he', Odysseus, and σφίσιν 'to them', his parents. κατέλεξεν is the aorist of καταλέγω 'recount in full', and εὖ 'well, fully' adds that he told it all. ὥς … ἔλασεν σῦς is an indirect statement, 'how a boar struck', with μιν 'him' as its object and the accusative participles θηρεύοντ’ 'hunting' and ἐλθόντα 'having gone' agreeing with it. λευκῷ ὀδόντι is 'with a white tooth', the boar's tusk (the same word as ὀδόντι at 450). Παρνησόνδ’ is 'to Parnassus' (-δε). υἱάσιν is an unusual dative plural of υἱός 'son' (Attic υἱέσι).

sentences.t:
τὴν γρηῢς χείρεσσι καταπρηνέσσι λαβοῦσα
γνῶ ῥ’ ἐπιμασσαμένη, πόδα δὲ προέηκε φέρεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
tēn grēÿs cheiressi kataprēnessi labousa
gnō rh’ epimassamenē, poda de proeēke pheresthai·
sentences.l:
It the old woman with downturned hands having taken
recognised, having felt it over, and the foot she let go to be carried;
sentences.i: Taking it in the flats of her hands, the old woman recognised it as she felt it over, and let the foot drop;
sentences.n: The story of the scar is over, and the scene returns to the foot-washing in the hall. τήν is 'it', the scar, which the old woman, γρηῦς (Eurycleia), takes in her hands; γρηῦς is the epic word for 'old woman' (Attic γραῦς). χείρεσσι καταπρηνέσσι is 'with downturned hands', that is with the flats of her hands (καταπρηνής 'bent down, flat'); ῥ’ is ἄρα. γνῶ is the aorist of γιγνώσκω 'recognise', without augment, and ἐπιμασσαμένη the aorist participle of ἐπιμαίομαι 'feel over, touch': the recognition comes by touch. πόδα … προέηκε φέρεσθαι is 'she let the foot go to fall' (προέηκε is the aorist of προΐημι 'let go, send forth', and the middle infinitive φέρεσθαι 'to be carried').

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ λέβητι πέσε κνήμη, κανάχησε δὲ χαλκός,
ἂψ δ’ ἑτέρωσ’ ἐκλίθη·
sentences.tr:
en de lebēti pese knēmē, kanachēse de chalkos,
aps d’ heterōs’ eklithē·
sentences.l:
and into the cauldron fell the shin, and the bronze rang,
and back to the other side it tilted;
sentences.i: the shin fell into the cauldron and the bronze rang out, and the cauldron tipped back and over to the other side;
sentences.n: The dropped leg overturns the bath. ἐν … πέσε is a tmesis of ἔμπεσε 'fell into', with δέ standing between preverb and verb; κνήμη is the shin, and λέβης 'cauldron' is the basin in which she was washing his feet. κανάχησε is the aorist of a verb meaning 'ring, clang', a sound-word, and χαλκός 'bronze' is the vessel itself. ἐκλίθη is the aorist passive of κλίνω 'lean, tilt'; no subject is stated, and the cauldron is understood. ἂψ δ’ ἑτέρωσε is 'and back to the other side'. The unit ends mid-line.

sentences.t: τὸ δ’ ἐπὶ χθονὸς ἐξέχυθ’ ὕδωρ.
sentences.tr: to d’ epi chthonos exechyth’ hydōr.
sentences.l: and the water was poured out on the ground.
sentences.i: and the water spilled out onto the ground.
sentences.n: The water is lost. τό is the old demonstrative, here close to the article 'the', with ὕδωρ 'water'; ἐξέχυθ’ is ἐξεχύθη, the aorist passive of ἐκχέω 'pour out', and ἐπὶ χθονός is 'on the ground' (χθών 'earth, ground'). The unit begins in the middle of line 470.

sentences.t:
τὴν δ’ ἅμα χάρμα καὶ ἄλγος ἕλε φρένα, τὼ δέ οἱ ὄσσε
δακρυόφι πλῆσθεν, θαλερὴ δέ οἱ ἔσχετο φωνή.
sentences.tr:
tēn d’ hama charma kai algos hele phrena, tō de hoi osse
dakryophi plēsthen, thalerē de hoi escheto phōnē.
sentences.l:
And her at once joy and pain seized in her mind, and her two eyes
were filled with tears, and her full voice was checked.
sentences.i: Joy and pain seized her mind together, and her eyes filled with tears, and her strong voice was choked.
sentences.n: Eurycleia's reaction to what she has found: joy and pain together. τὴν … φρένα is 'her … in the mind', both accusatives, the person and the part affected; ἅμα is 'at once', χάρμα 'joy' and ἄλγος 'pain', and ἕλε is the aorist of αἱρέω, here 'seized'. τὼ δέ οἱ ὄσσε: τώ is the dual of the article, 'the two', ὄσσε the dual 'eyes', and οἱ 'her'. δακρυόφι 'with tears' has the old case-ending -φι, and πλῆσθεν is the unaugmented aorist passive of πίμπλημι 'fill'. θαλερὴ … φωνή is 'full voice' (θαλερός 'blooming, strong'); ἔσχετο is the aorist middle of ἔχω, 'was held back'.

sentences.t: ἁψαμένη δὲ γενείου Ὀδυσσῆα προσέειπεν·
sentences.tr: hapsamenē de geneiou Odyssēa proseeipen·
sentences.l: And having laid hold of his chin, Odysseus she addressed:
sentences.i: She took Odysseus by the chin and said to him:
sentences.n: A gesture of closeness precedes the words. ἁψαμένη is the aorist middle participle of ἅπτω 'touch, take hold of', with the genitive γενείου 'chin'. Ὀδυσσῆα is the object of προσέειπεν 'addressed' (Attic προσεῖπεν), and the speech that follows is Eurycleia's.

sentences.t: ἦ μάλ’ Ὀδυσσεύς ἐσσι, φίλον τέκος·
sentences.tr: ē mal’ Odysseus essi, philon tekos·
sentences.l: “Truly Odysseus you are, dear child;
sentences.i: “You are truly Odysseus, dear child;
sentences.n: Eurycleia speaks, and these are the words of recognition. ἦ μάλα is 'truly, indeed', and ἐσσι the epic form of εἶ 'you are'. τέκος is 'child' (neuter; Attic τέκνον), and φίλον 'dear' agrees with it. She says it without hedging: touch has told her what she could not see.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ σ’ ἐγώ γε
πρὶν ἔγνων, πρὶν πάντα ἄνακτ’ ἐμὸν ἀμφαφάασθαι.
sentences.tr:
oude s’ egō ge
prin egnōn, prin panta anakt’ emon amphaphaasthai.
sentences.l:
and you I, for my part, did not
recognise, before I had handled my lord all over.”
sentences.i: and I did not recognise you until I had felt my lord all over.”
sentences.n: She explains how she knew him, and her speech ends. οὐδέ 'and not' continues from the last unit; ἔγνων is the aorist of γιγνώσκω 'recognise', and ἐγώ γε 'I for my part'. The first πρίν is the adverb 'sooner', answered by the second: πρίν … ἀμφαφάασθαι is 'before … feeling over', with the infinitive after πρίν; ἀμφαφάασθαι is the stretched form of ἀμφαφᾶσθαι, the middle infinitive of ἀμφαφάω 'feel all over, handle'. πάντα … ἄνακτ’ ἐμόν is 'my lord entirely' (ἄνακτ’ is the elided accusative of ἄναξ 'lord, master'). The unit begins in the middle of line 474.

sentences.t:
ἦ καὶ Πηνελόπειαν ἐσέδρακεν ὀφθαλμοῖσι,
πεφραδέειν ἐθέλουσα φίλον πόσιν ἔνδον ἐόντα.
sentences.tr:
ē kai Pēnelopeian esedraken ophthalmoisi,
pephradeein ethelousa philon posin endon eonta.
sentences.l:
She spoke, and at Penelope she looked with her eyes,
wishing to point out her dear husband to be within.
sentences.i: So she said, and fixed her eyes on Penelope, wanting to show her that her dear husband was there inside.
sentences.n: Eurycleia turns from Odysseus to Penelope and tries to tell her with a look. ἦ καί is 'so she spoke, and' (ἦ is the old verb ἠμί 'say', used after a speech). ἐσέδρακεν is the aorist of εἰσδέρκομαι 'look at', with ὀφθαλμοῖσι 'with her eyes'. πεφραδέειν is the reduplicated aorist infinitive of φράζω 'point out, show', and ἐθέλουσα 'wishing'. φίλον πόσιν ἔνδον ἐόντα is an accusative phrase, 'her dear husband being within': what she wants to show is that he is in the room. ἐόντα is Attic ὄντα.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ οὔτ’ ἀθρῆσαι δύνατ’ ἀντίη οὔτε νοῆσαι·
sentences.tr: hē d’ out’ athrēsai dynat’ antiē oute noēsai·
sentences.l: But she was neither able to catch sight, face to face, nor to understand;
sentences.i: But Penelope, though she faced them, could neither see nor understand;
sentences.n: Penelope does not take it in. ἡ δέ 'but she' is Penelope. ἀθρῆσαι is the aorist infinitive of ἀθρέω 'catch sight of, observe', and νοῆσαι the aorist infinitive of νοέω 'perceive, understand'; both depend on δύνατ’ (δύνατο, the imperfect of δύναμαι). ἀντίη 'face to face, opposite' agrees with ἡ, so she is directly in front of them and still cannot notice what passes. No object is stated for either verb, and the English leaves it open too. The reason comes in the next line.

sentences.t: τῇ γὰρ Ἀθηναίη νόον ἔτραπεν·
sentences.tr: tēi gar Athēnaiē noon etrapen·
sentences.l: for to her Athena her mind had turned;
sentences.i: for Athena had turned her mind aside;
sentences.n: The reason (γάρ). τῇ is the pronoun 'to her', Penelope, and νόον ἔτραπεν is 'turned her mind', the aorist of τρέπω; the English past perfect shows that it was done before. The Greek has no preverb, and 'aside' is the sense the context gives. Ἀθηναίη is the Homeric form of Ἀθηνᾶ, and νόος (contracted νοῦς) is 'mind, thought', the faculty of noticing.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
χεῖρ’ ἐπιμασσάμενος φάρυγος λάβε δεξιτερῆφι,
τῇ δ’ ἑτέρῃ ἕθεν ἆσσον ἐρύσσατο φώνησέν τε.
sentences.tr:
autar Odysseus
cheir’ epimassamenos pharygos labe dexiterēphi,
tēi d’ heterēi hethen asson eryssato phōnēsen te.
sentences.l:
but Odysseus
his hand having reached out, her throat took hold of with his right,
and with the other nearer to himself drew her, and spoke:
sentences.i: but Odysseus reached out his hand and seized her by the throat with his right, and with the other drew her closer to himself, and spoke:
sentences.n: Odysseus acts at once to keep Eurycleia silent. αὐτάρ is 'but'. χεῖρ’ ἐπιμασσάμενος is 'having put out his hand' (the aorist participle of ἐπιμαίομαι 'reach for, feel for', the verb of 468, here with χεῖρα as its object). φάρυγος is the genitive of φάρυξ 'throat' after λάβε, the aorist of λαμβάνω 'take hold of', and δεξιτερῆφι 'with the right (hand)' has the old ending -φι. τῇ δ’ ἑτέρῃ is 'with the other' (hand understood). ἕθεν is the reflexive genitive 'of himself', and ἆσσον 'nearer' goes with it: 'nearer to himself'. ἐρύσσατο is the aorist middle of ἐρύω 'draw', and φώνησέν τε 'and spoke' is the same pair of words as at 405.

sentences.t: μαῖα, τίη μ’ ἐθέλεις ὀλέσαι;
sentences.tr: maia, tiē m’ etheleis olesai;
sentences.l: “Nurse, why do you wish to destroy me?
sentences.i: “Nurse, why do you want to destroy me?
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks. μαῖα is the address 'nurse', a familiar word for an older woman. τίη is τί 'why'; ἐθέλεις takes the aorist infinitive ὀλέσαι 'to destroy' (ὄλλυμι), and the question means 'why are you trying to ruin me?', since a cry or a look from her would give him away.

sentences.t:
σὺ δέ μ’ ἔτρεφες αὐτὴ
τῷ σῷ ἐπὶ μαζῷ·
sentences.tr:
sy de m’ etrephes autē
tōi sōi epi mazōi·
sentences.l:
But you yourself nursed me
at your own breast;
sentences.i: And yet you yourself nursed me at your own breast;
sentences.n: σὺ δέ 'but you' sets her care of him against her present danger to him. ἔτρεφες is the imperfect of τρέφω 'nurse, rear', and αὐτή 'yourself' has the feminine ending. ἐπὶ μαζῷ is 'at the breast' (μαζός, in the dative), with τῷ σῷ 'your own' (the article with the possessive). The unit begins in the middle of line 482.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἄλγεα πολλὰ μογήσας
ἤλυθον εἰκοστῷ ἔτεϊ ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ algea polla mogēsas
ēlython eikostōi eteï es patrida gaian.
sentences.l:
but now, many pains having suffered,
I have come in the twentieth year to my fatherland.
sentences.i: and now, after suffering many pains, I have come in the twentieth year to my fatherland.
sentences.n: νῦν δέ 'but now' contrasts the nursing of long ago with the present. ἄλγεα πολλὰ μογήσας is 'having suffered many pains' (μογέω 'toil, suffer hardship'). ἤλυθον is the Homeric aorist of ἔρχομαι, 'I came', and the English perfect is the one used for the same words elsewhere. εἰκοστῷ ἔτεϊ is 'in the twentieth year', a dative of time, and ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν is 'to my fatherland'. The unit begins in the middle of line 483.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ ἐφράσθης καί τοι θεὸς ἔμβαλε θυμῷ,
σίγα, μή τίς τ’ ἄλλος ἐνὶ μεγάροισι πύθηται.
sentences.tr:
all’ epei ephrasthēs kai toi theos embale thymōi,
siga, mē tis t’ allos eni megaroisi pythētai.
sentences.l:
But since you noticed, and to you a god cast it into your heart,
be silent, lest any other in the halls learn of it.
sentences.i: But since you have noticed it, and a god has put it into your heart, keep silent, so that no one else in the halls finds out.
sentences.n: The command: be quiet. ἀλλ’ ἐπεί 'but since' gives the ground for the command. ἐφράσθης is the aorist, in passive form, of φράζομαι 'notice, perceive', and καί τοι θεὸς ἔμβαλε θυμῷ is 'and a god put it in your heart' (τοι 'to you', ἔμβαλε 'threw in', θυμῷ the dative 'heart'): the recognition is a thought a god put there. σίγα is the imperative of σιγάω 'be silent'. μή τις … πύθηται is a negative purpose clause ('lest') after the imperative, with the aorist subjunctive of πυνθάνομαι 'find out'; τε after τίς is an epic particle that need not be translated. ἐνὶ μεγάροισι 'in the halls' is a plural for one house.

sentences.t: ὧδε γὰρ ἐξερέω, καὶ μὴν τετελεσμένον ἔσται·
sentences.tr: hōde gar exereō, kai mēn tetelesmenon estai·
sentences.l: for thus I will declare, and truly accomplished it will be;
sentences.i: For this I will declare, and it will surely be accomplished:
sentences.n: He tells her what will happen, in the three lines that follow. ὧδε is 'thus' and looks forward to them; ἐξερέω is the future 'I will declare'. καὶ μὴν 'and truly' introduces a solemn assertion. τετελεσμένον ἔσται is 'it will be a thing accomplished', the perfect passive participle of τελέω with the future of εἰμί: the threat is meant seriously and will be carried out.

sentences.t:
εἴ χ’ ὑπ’ ἐμοί γε θεὸς δαμάσῃ μνηστῆρας ἀγαυούς,
οὐδὲ τροφοῦ οὔσης σεῦ ἀφέξομαι, ὁππότ’ ἂν ἄλλας
δμῳὰς ἐν μεγάροισιν ἐμοῖς κτείνωμι γυναῖκας.
sentences.tr:
ei ch’ hyp’ emoi ge theos damasēi mnēstēras agauous,
oude trophou ousēs seu aphexomai, hoppot’ an allas
dmōias en megaroisin emois kteinōmi gynaikas.
sentences.i: If a god overcomes the noble suitors at my hands, I will not spare even you, nurse though you are, when I kill the other women, the maids, in my halls.”
sentences.n: Odysseus warns his nurse that he will not spare even her when he kills the disloyal women; the condition, that she must keep silent, is understood and not stated, and his speech ends. εἴ χ’ is εἴ κε, with the aorist subjunctive δαμάσῃ 'subdues' ('if ever a god subdues'); ὑπ’ ἐμοί (ὑπό with the dative) is 'under me', so 'at my hands'; μνηστῆρας ἀγαυούς is 'the noble suitors' by the house rendering of ἀγαυός. τροφοῦ οὔσης σεῦ is 'you being a nurse': the participle οὔσης agrees with σεῦ, the genitive object of ἀφέξομαι 'I shall keep off', which takes the genitive; οὐδέ is 'not even'. ὁππότ’ ἄν with the subjunctive κτείνωμι is 'whenever I kill', δμῳάς 'maidservants', ἄλλας 'other', and ἐμοῖς 'my'; γυναῖκας 'women' is in apposition to δμῳάς.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Εὐρύκλεια·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe periphrōn Eurykleia·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed circumspect Eurycleia:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Eurycleia spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is a reply-formula: τόν is the pronoun 'him', αὖτε 'in turn', and προσέειπε the uncontracted aorist 'addressed' (Attic προσεῖπε). περίφρων is 'circumspect', from περί 'round, all round' and φρήν 'mind', and the epithet comes with the name Εὐρύκλεια at the end of the line. Her speech runs to 498.

sentences.t: τέκνον ἐμόν, ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων.
sentences.tr: teknon emon, poion se epos phygen herkos odontōn.
sentences.l: “My child, what a word has escaped you, the fence of your teeth.
sentences.i: “My child, what a word is this that has got past the fence of your teeth!
sentences.n: Eurycleia begins by rebuking his threat. τέκνον ἐμόν is 'my child'. ποῖον … ἔπος 'what sort of word' is an exclamation, and φύγεν is the unaugmented aorist of φεύγω 'escape', with σε 'you' as the one it escaped. ἕρκος ὀδόντων 'the fence of the teeth' is the Greek picture of the teeth as an enclosure that words should not leave.

sentences.t:
οἶσθα μὲν οἷον ἐμὸν μένος ἔμπεδον οὐδ’ ἐπιεικτόν,
ἕξω δ’ ὡς ὅτε τις στερεὴ λίθος ἠὲ σίδηρος.
sentences.tr:
oistha men hoion emon menos empedon oud’ epieikton,
hexō d’ hōs hote tis stereē lithos ēe sidēros.
sentences.l:
You know indeed what sort my strength is, firm and unyielding,
and I will hold out like some hard stone or iron.
sentences.i: You know how firm my strength is, and how unyielding; I will hold out like some hard stone or iron.
sentences.n: She promises silence by comparing herself to stone. μέν is answered by δέ in the next line: 'you know …, and I will hold'. οἶσθα is 'you know' (οἶδα), and οἷον is 'what sort', introducing an indirect exclamation. μένος is 'strength' by the house rendering; ἔμπεδον is 'firm', and ἐπιεικτόν, from ἐπείκω 'yield', 'yielding', with οὐδ’ 'nor': 'not yielding'. ἕξω is the future of ἔχω, 'I shall hold out'; ὡς ὅτε τις 'as when some' introduces the comparison, στερεή 'hard, firm' agrees with λίθος 'stone', and σίδηρος is 'iron'.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσιν·
sentences.tr: allo de toi ereō, sy d’ eni phresi balleo sēisin·
sentences.l: And another thing to you I will say, and you in your own mind lay it:
sentences.i: And I will tell you something else; lay it up in your own mind:
sentences.n: She has a second thing to say, and she asks him to take it to heart. ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω is 'and another thing I will tell you': ἄλλο is 'another thing', τοι 'to you' (= σοι), and ἐρέω the future 'I will say'. βάλλεο is a middle imperative of βάλλω with the ending -εο, 'put for yourself, lay up'; ἐνὶ φρεσί is 'in the mind', and σῇσιν is the possessive 'your own' in the long dative ending -ῃσιν.

sentences.t:
εἴ χ’ ὑπό σοι γε θεὸς δαμάσῃ μνηστῆρας ἀγαυούς,
δὴ τότε τοι καταλέξω ἐνὶ μεγάροισι γυναῖκας,
αἵ τέ σ’ ἀτιμάζουσι καὶ αἳ νηλείτιδές εἰσι.
sentences.tr:
ei ch’ hypo soi ge theos damasēi mnēstēras agauous,
dē tote toi katalexō eni megaroisi gynaikas,
hai te s’ atimazousi kai hai nēleitides eisi.
sentences.l:
If under you, at least, a god subdues the noble suitors,
then indeed to you I will recount the women in the halls,
both those who dishonour you and who are guiltless.”
sentences.i: If a god overcomes the noble suitors at your hands, then I will recount to you the women in the halls, which of them dishonour you, and which are guiltless.”
sentences.n: Her offer: when the suitors are dead she will name the women of the household who have wronged him, and her speech ends. The first line repeats Odysseus's own at 488, with σοι 'you' for ἐμοί, and the English repeats too. δὴ τότε is 'then indeed', and καταλέξω is the future of καταλέγω 'recount in full, list'. αἵ τε … καὶ αἵ … is 'both those who … and those who …': ἀτιμάζουσι is 'dishonour' (treat as of no account), and νηλείτιδες is 'guiltless', the feminine plural of an adjective meaning one who owes no penalty.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: A reply-formula with the speaker's name at the end. τὴν … ἀπαμειβόμενος is 'answering her', with the participle in place of the finite verb of 405; προσέφη is 'addressed'. πολύμητις 'many-wiled' is Odysseus's epithet, from πολύς 'much' and μῆτις 'cunning intelligence, craft', translated each time. The next unit begins his speech.

sentences.t: μαῖα, τίη δὲ σὺ τὰς μυθήσεαι;
sentences.tr: maia, tiē de sy tas mythēseai;
sentences.l: “Nurse, but why will you tell of them?
sentences.i: “Nurse, why should you tell of them?
sentences.n: Odysseus answers her offer. μαῖα 'nurse' is the address again. τίη δέ is 'but why', and σύ is emphatic, 'you'. τάς is the pronoun 'them', the women she has offered to list, and μυθήσεαι is the future of μυθέομαι 'tell, speak of' (uncontracted -εαι); a future in a question like this is close to 'why should you?'.

sentences.t: οὐδέ τί σε χρή.
sentences.tr: oude ti se chrē.
sentences.l: Nor is there any need for you.
sentences.i: There is no need at all for you.
sentences.n: οὐδέ τί σε χρή is 'nor is there any need for you': χρή 'it is necessary' takes the accusative of the person (σε), and its infinitive is left out here, 'to tell'. τί is the adverb 'at all'. The unit begins in the middle of line 500.

sentences.t: εὖ νυ καὶ αὐτὸς ἐγὼ φράσομαι καὶ εἴσομ’ ἑκάστην·
sentences.tr: eu ny kai autos egō phrasomai kai eisom’ hekastēn·
sentences.l: Well now, I myself will take note, and I shall know each one;
sentences.i: I shall observe them well enough myself, and I shall know each one of them;
sentences.n: He means that he will see for himself which of the women are at fault. εὖ is 'well', and νυ the particle 'now' (= νῦν), which softens the statement; καὶ αὐτὸς ἐγώ is 'I myself too'. φράσομαι is the future of φράζομαι 'observe, take note', and εἴσομ’ the elided future of οἶδα 'I shall know'. ἑκάστην is 'each one', in the feminine, each of the women.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔχε σιγῇ μῦθον, ἐπίτρεψον δὲ θεοῖσιν.
sentences.tr: all’ eche sigēi mython, epitrepson de theoisin.
sentences.l: but hold the speech in silence, and entrust it to the gods.”
sentences.i: but keep the matter in silence, and leave it to the gods.”
sentences.n: He ends with the same demand for silence, now with the outcome left to the gods. ἔχε is the imperative of ἔχω 'hold, keep', σιγῇ 'in silence' (the dative of σιγή), and μῦθον here 'the word, the matter', what she has just learned. ἐπίτρεψον is the aorist imperative of ἐπιτρέπω 'entrust, hand over', with δέ 'and' and the dative θεοῖσιν 'to the gods'.
